data.name: Tuning_Note
data.value: GPU overclock, undervolt, power limit and fan through NVIDIA's own management library (NVML). Every setting is volatile: a restart or a driver reset puts the card back to stock. Values outside the driver's ranges are refused.

data.name: Tuning_Manual_Note
data.value: NVIDIA's public interface does not set a voltage directly. An undervolt is a positive core offset together with a clock cap: the offset lifts the voltage/frequency curve, the cap keeps the clock where it was, so the card reaches that clock at a lower voltage. An overclock is a higher cap (or no cap) with an offset.

data.name: Tuning_Hint_Fan

data.name: Tuning_Auto_Note
data.value: Automatic undervolt measures the card at stock under a verified GPU load, then raises the offset step by step at the same clock until it computes wrongly, the driver resets, or the clock drops; it backs off a margin and confirms with a long run. Automatic overclock starts from the undervolt and raises the clock cap, then the memory offset, while the card stays correct, gets faster and draws no more power than at stock. A result is saved as a profile only when the measurements beat stock. Takes about 10–25 minutes; the screen may flicker or go black for a moment if the driver resets. Close games and save your work first.

data.name: Tuning_Profiles_Note

data.name: Tuning_Memory_Note

data.name: Advice_Cpu
data.value: Seen: the CPU computed wrong results under load. Likely causes: an overclock, undervolt or Curve Optimizer setting that is not stable; too little voltage or a weak VRM; overheating; unstable RAM (the matrix and Linpack loads also use memory). Next: reset the BIOS to defaults and repeat; watch the temperature in the report; run single-core cycling to find the core; test the RAM on its own.

data.name: Advice_Memory
data.value: Seen: data read back from RAM differed from what was written. Likely causes: a faulty module; the memory controller in the CPU; an XMP or manual memory setting that is not stable; the slot or the board. Next: set the memory to its JEDEC speed (XMP off) and repeat; test one module at a time and swap slots; for full coverage run MemTest86 from a USB stick, outside Windows.

data.name: Advice_Gpu
data.value: Seen: the graphics card computed or drew wrong results, or its device was lost. Likely causes: a core or memory overclock; overheating (see the hot spot); the power supply or its cables; the driver. Next: return the card to stock clocks and repeat; check the hot-spot temperature; reinstall the driver cleanly; run the combined power test to load the power supply.

data.name: Advice_Vram
data.value: Seen: the graphics card's memory returned data different from what was written. Likely causes: a memory overclock; VRAM overheating (see the memory junction temperature); faulty memory chips. Next: return the memory clock to stock and repeat; check the VRAM temperature and the card's cooling; if it fails at stock and cool, the card needs service.

data.name: Advice_Storage
data.value: Seen: the drive returned wrong or short data, or an I/O error, while being written and read. Likely causes: the drive's media or controller; the cable or port (SATA); the board's controller or its driver; the power to the drive. Next: read SMART and the storage events in this report; try another cable and port; repeat on another machine if you can. Back up the data first.

data.name: Advice_Smart
data.value: Seen: Windows reports the drive's own health as failing, or it counts uncorrected errors. Likely causes: the drive itself, reported by its own monitoring. Next: back up the data now; plan to replace the drive; the storage tests can show whether reads and writes still come back right.

data.name: Advice_Network
data.value: Seen: too many echo requests were lost. Likely causes: the cable or Wi-Fi signal; the router or the target; the adapter's driver. Next: ping the router (gateway) to separate the local link from the internet; try another cable, port or target.

data.name: Advice_Power
data.value: Seen: a fault appeared while the CPU and the graphics card were loaded together. Likely causes: the power supply; the board's VRM; the cooling of the case under full heat. This test cannot measure the power supply itself. Next: run the CPU and GPU tests one at a time: a fault only together points at power or heat; try a known good power supply.

data.name: Advice_Windows
data.value: Seen: Windows found damaged system files it could not repair. Likely causes: an interrupted update; disk errors; failing storage or RAM. Next: run DISM /RestoreHealth on the Windows Tools page, then sfc again; test the RAM and the Windows drive.

data.name: Advice_Inconclusive
data.value: No error was seen, but the test could not cover everything it was asked to; the result is neither a pass nor a fail. See the detail for what was left out, and repeat with more time.

data.name: Advice_Inconclusive_Cores
data.value: No core computed wrongly, but not every core was tested (the time ran out, or Windows would not keep the thread on a core). Give each core at least a few seconds: the length should be at least the number of cores × seconds per core.

data.name: Advice_Inconclusive_Network
data.value: Not one echo reply came back. A firewall or the target may drop ICMP - that is not a fault of the network card. Ping the router or another target; the internet speed benchmark checks the connection another way.

data.name: Advice_Error
data.value: The test itself stopped with a program error; nothing is known about the part from this run. Repeat it; if it happens again, send the app's log (Settings) to the shop.

data.value: The models run in llama.cpp (open source, MIT), downloaded once from its official GitHub release and checked against its checksum. Its Vulkan build runs on NVIDIA, AMD and Intel graphics cards and on the processor.

data.name: Ai_NeedRuntime
data.value: Download llama.cpp above to run this model.

data.name: Ai_HowTo
data.value: Fit is an estimate made before downloading: the model's weights, its cache for 4,096 tokens of text and the runtime's working memory, against this machine's video memory and free RAM (1 GB of each is left free, as llama.cpp does). Speed is measured, never estimated: llama.cpp's own benchmark (llama-bench) reads a 512-token prompt, then writes 128 tokens, three times each. Generation is how fast the answer is written. A token is a piece of a word; at about 10 tokens a second the answer appears as fast as you read it. Prompt processing is how fast the question and any documents given to the model are read: it sets the wait before the first word. Nothing is downloaded until you press Download. Models come from Hugging Face (ggml-org, the llama.cpp project) and are checked against their published checksums.

data.name: Ai_Purpose_Qwen35_08
data.value: The smallest and fastest. Runs on almost any computer, even on a laptop's processor. For short, simple jobs: sorting text, short summaries, quick answers. Weak at reasoning and long answers.

data.name: Ai_Purpose_Qwen3_4
data.value: A light everyday assistant: chat, writing, summaries and simple code, with a thinking mode for step-by-step answers. Runs wholly on a card with 4 to 6 GB and is usable on a strong processor.

data.name: Ai_Purpose_Qwen3_14
data.value: Clearly better than the small ones at reasoning, coding and following instructions. Needs a card with 12 GB or more for full speed; on 8 GB it is split with the RAM and slows down.

data.name: Ai_Purpose_GptOss20
data.value: OpenAI's open model, a mixture of experts: 21 billion parameters, of which only 3.6 billion work on each token, so it writes about as fast as a small model while knowing much more. Good at reasoning and at using tools. Needs 16 GB of video memory, or runs split with the RAM.

data.name: Ai_Purpose_Qwen38_27
data.value: The most capable model in this list: for hard questions, long code and careful writing. Every token reads all of its 19 GB of weights, so it needs a 24 GB card and is the slowest here.

data.name: Ai_Purpose_Qwen36_35
data.value: The knowledge of a large model at the speed of a small one: 35 billion parameters, 3 billion active per token. It runs whole on a 24 GB card; with less, part of it goes to the RAM and it stays usable, since few weights are read for each token.

data.value: What only a person can judge: dead pixels, keys, speakers, microphone and mouse. Each check shows exactly what the computer received; you make the call.

data.name: Checks_Display_Text
data.value: The screen fills with black, white, red, green, blue and grey, then a gradient and a fine checkerboard. Look closely for a dot that stays dark or lit, uneven light at the edges, or steps in the gradient.

data.name: Checks_Display_Hint
data.value: Click or any key: next colour · right click or ←: back · Esc: end

data.name: Checks_Keys_Text
data.value: Press Start, then every key once: a key turns green when the computer receives it and yellow while it is held. A key that stays yellow after release is stuck. The Windows key and some laptop Fn keys go to Windows first and may not show.

data.name: Checks_Speakers_Text
data.value: A 440 Hz tone on the left, on both sides, or on the right; the left one must come only from the left. The sweep runs from 20 Hz to 20 kHz in 10 seconds: listen for a rattle, a buzz or a range where the sound drops out.

data.name: Checks_Mic_Text
data.value: Speak or tap near the microphone: the bar shows the level the default recording device delivers, without Windows' noise suppression. Silence should sit low and steady; speech should move it clearly.

data.name: Checks_Mouse_Text
data.value: Press each button inside the box and turn the wheel both ways. Each press is counted once: a button whose count jumps by two for one press double-clicks by itself, a common fault of worn switches.

Likely causes: the network cable or a port; the network card, its driver or its offload settings; the switch or router between them; unstable RAM on either computer. Next: repeat with another cable and port; connect the two computers directly; update or reinstall the network driver; test the RAM of both computers.

data.name: Checkup_Lede
data.value: Whether this machine works as it should, judged from its own measurements: the setup as it is now, and every CPU and graphics benchmark run in this session, against what its parts report themselves and against other systems with the same parts.

data.name: Checkup_RunHint
data.value: Runs the CPU (all cores and one core), memory and graphics benchmarks one after another. Close other programs first.

data.name: Checkup_NoRuns
data.value: No CPU or graphics benchmark has run in this session yet. Run the checkup, or any of them on the Benchmarks page, and its findings appear here.

data.name: Checkup_Summary_Good
data.value: No problem found in what was checked.

data.name: Checkup_Nothing
data.value: Nothing to judge in this run: the sensors it needs gave no readings.

data.name: Check_CpuNotFullyLoaded
data.value: The CPU was not fully loaded

data.name: Check_CpuNotFullyLoaded_Text
data.value: Another program used the processor during the run, so its clock and heat are not judged. Close other programs and run it again.

data.name: Check_CpuStuckLowClock
data.value: The CPU is held under 1 GHz

data.name: Check_CpuStuckLowClock_Text
data.value: Under full load the processor never went above 1 GHz: something is holding it down. On a laptop it is most often a faulty, fake or too weak charger (the board then raises BD PROCHOT and keeps the CPU at its lowest clock), a worn battery or a failing power circuit; on any machine, the power plan or a BIOS setting. Try the original charger first, then check the power plan and the BIOS.

data.name: Check_CpuBelowBaseClock
data.value: All-core clock below the base clock

data.name: Check_CpuBelowBaseClock_Text
data.value: Under all-core load the clock fell below the base clock the processor is rated to hold. The usual causes are cooling that cannot keep up, a power limit set below the processor's rating (common on thin laptops), or weak power delivery on the board.

data.name: Check_CpuAtTjMax
data.value: The CPU reached its temperature limit

data.name: Check_CpuAtTjMax_Text
data.value: The processor reached the limit it reports itself (TjMax), where it lowers its clock to protect itself. Some high-end processors run up to it by design under a long all-core load, but if the clock fell a lot the cooling is not enough: check the cooler's mounting and paste, its fan or pump, and the case airflow.

data.name: Check_CpuNearTjMax_Text
data.value: The processor ran close to its own limit but did not reach it, so heat did not hold it back in this run. A longer load or a warmer room may bring it to the limit.

data.name: Check_CpuHeldAtCeiling
data.value: The CPU is held at its temperature ceiling

data.name: Check_CpuHeldAtCeiling_Text
data.value: The temperature sat flat at its top while the clock kept falling: the processor holds its temperature limit by giving up clock. Processors such as AMD's Ryzen stop at their limit (95 °C on many models) and lower the clock instead of getting hotter, so the degree alone says little; the falling clock shows the cooling is not keeping up. Check the cooler's mounting and paste, its fan or pump, and the case airflow.

data.name: Check_CpuHotSteady_Text
data.value: The temperature stayed flat near its top but the clock did not fall, so heat did not hold the processor back in this run. Many current processors are built to boost until they reach their temperature limit.

data.name: Check_CpuHeatOk_Text
data.value: The temperature stayed below where the processor slows itself.

data.name: Check_CpuPowerStep
data.value: A short boost, then a lower power limit

data.name: Check_CpuPowerStep_Text
data.value: For the first seconds the processor drew more power, then dropped to a lower, steady level while the temperature still had room. That is the power limits set in the BIOS or by the laptop's maker (a short-term and a long-term one), not a fault. Intel's default settings on Core 13th and 14th gen work this way and keep the P-cores under 5 GHz in long all-core work; a board's unlimited or undervolted setting gives more clock, and more heat.

data.name: Check_PowerPlanCap
data.value: The power plan caps the processor

data.name: Check_PowerPlanCap_Text
data.value: The active power plan's maximum processor state is under 100 %. Under 100 % Windows keeps the processor at or below its base clock, so it never boosts. Set it back to 100 % (Control Panel, Power Options, the plan's advanced settings, Processor power management).

data.name: Check_PowerPlanNoBoost
data.value: Boost is turned off in the power plan

data.name: Check_PowerPlanNoBoost_Text
data.value: The power plan's processor boost mode is set to Disabled, so the processor stays at its base clock. It is a hidden setting some optimisation tools change: set it back to Enabled or Aggressive (with powercfg), or restore the plan's defaults.

data.name: Check_PowerOnBattery_Text
data.value: The machine runs on battery. Laptops cut the processor's and the graphics card's power on battery; benchmark a laptop with its charger in.

data.name: Check_PowerPlanOk
data.value: The power plan does not hold the processor

data.name: Check_PowerPlanOk_Text
data.value: The power plan lets the processor run at its full clock, with boost.

data.name: Check_RamXmpOff
data.value: Memory runs below its rated speed (XMP off)

data.name: Check_RamXmpOff_Text
data.value: The modules carry an XMP profile for a higher speed, but the memory runs at its standard speed. Turn on XMP in the BIOS (some boards call it DOCP or EXPO). If the system is unstable with it, the board or the processor may not hold that speed.

data.name: Check_RamXmpOn
data.value: Memory runs at its XMP speed

data.name: Check_RamXmpOn_Text
data.value: The memory runs at the speed of the modules' XMP profile.

data.name: Check_RamBelowJedec
data.value: Memory runs below its standard speed

data.name: Check_RamBelowJedec_Text
data.value: The memory runs slower than the modules' own standard (JEDEC) speed. The board or the processor may not support that speed, or with four modules the board lowered it; otherwise set it in the BIOS.

data.name: Check_RamAtJedec
data.value: Memory runs at its standard speed

data.name: Check_RamAtJedec_Text
data.value: The memory runs at the modules' fastest standard (JEDEC) speed; they carry no faster profile.

data.name: Check_RamProfileUnread
data.value: The memory's rated speed was not read

data.name: Check_RamProfileUnread_Text
data.value: This version does not read the rated speed of DDR5 modules yet, so whether XMP or EXPO is on is not judged. Compare the speed in the BIOS with the one on the modules' label.

data.name: Check_RamSingleChannel_Text
data.value: With one module the memory runs in a single channel, at half the bandwidth of two. Games and integrated graphics suffer most. A second identical module fixes it.

data.name: Check_RamSameChannel_Text
data.value: By their slot names, all the modules sit in one channel, so the memory runs single-channel. Move them to the slots the board's manual gives for two modules (usually A2 and B2).

data.name: Check_RamMixed_Text
data.value: The modules are not all the same model or size. Mixed modules run at the slowest one's speed and timings, and a different size can leave part of the memory in a single channel.

data.name: Check_GpuPowerBrake_Text
data.value: The card's driver reported that an external power brake cut its clock. This comes from the power side: a power supply that cannot deliver, a loose or damaged power connector or cable, or an adapter. Check the cables and the power supply.

data.name: Check_GpuHwThermal_Text
data.value: The card's own protection cut its clock hard because part of it got too hot. Check the card's fans, its paste and thermal pads, and the case airflow.

data.name: Check_GpuHwSlowdown_Text
data.value: The card's driver reported a hardware slowdown (the clock cut by half or more) for a lasting part of the run. Its causes are too much heat, a power brake from the power supply, or power spikes the card's protection catches. Check the cooling, the cables and the power supply.

data.name: Check_GpuThermalSlowdown
data.value: The graphics card reached its temperature target

data.name: Check_GpuThermalSlowdown_Text
data.value: The driver lowered the card's clock because it reached its temperature target. Clean the card's fans and heatsink and check the case airflow; on an older card the paste and pads may need replacing.

data.name: Check_GpuPowerLimited
data.value: The graphics card runs at its power limit

data.name: Check_GpuPowerLimited_Text
data.value: Under full load the card ran at its power limit. That is how graphics cards are built to run, not a fault.

data.name: Check_GpuHeatOk
data.value: The graphics card was not held back by heat

data.name: Check_GpuHeatOk_Text
data.value: The card stayed below the temperature at which it slows itself.

data.name: Check_GpuHotspotGap
data.value: Hot spot far above the core

data.name: Check_GpuHotspotGap_Text
data.value: Under load the hottest spot of the chip ran much hotter than the core. That usually means dried paste or a cooler not pressing evenly on the chip; repasting (and checking the pads) usually fixes it.

data.name: Check_GpuLinkNarrow
data.value: Graphics card link narrower than it should be

data.name: Check_GpuLinkNarrow_Text
data.value: The card and the slot can both run more lanes than the link does. Reseat the card, clean the slot and the contacts, and check the riser cable if there is one; on some boards an M.2 drive shares lanes with this slot.

data.name: Check_GpuLinkSlowGen
data.value: Graphics card link at a lower PCIe generation

data.name: Check_GpuLinkSlowGen_Text
data.value: Under load the link ran at a lower PCIe generation than both the card and the slot support. Check the BIOS's PCIe setting (it may be fixed to a lower generation), the riser cable if any, and the card's seating.

data.name: Check_GpuSlotNarrow
data.value: The slot gives fewer lanes than the card can use

data.name: Check_GpuSlotNarrow_Text
data.value: The card runs at all the lanes its slot has. Most cards lose little at x8; a fast card loses more in a x4 slot. The board's main x16 slot, if free, is the better place.

data.name: Check_GpuSlotOlderGen
data.value: The slot is an older PCIe generation

data.name: Check_GpuSlotOlderGen_Text
data.value: The slot supports an older PCIe generation than the card, and the card runs at the slot's. That is normal for this board and costs most cards little.

data.name: Check_GpuLinkOk_Text
data.value: The card's PCIe link runs as wide, and as fast, as the card and the slot allow.

data.name: Check_GpuLinkBelowCard
data.value: The graphics card runs at fewer lanes than it supports

data.name: Check_GpuLinkBelowCard_Text
data.value: The card runs at fewer lanes than it supports; how many the slot provides could not be read on this machine. Many processors with integrated graphics (APUs) and secondary slots give only x8 or x4, which is normal. In a full x16 slot of a processor that has the lanes, reseat the card.

data.name: Check_DriveLinkNarrow
data.value: SSD link narrower than it should be

data.name: Check_DriveLinkNarrow_Text
data.value: The drive and its slot can both run more lanes than the link does. Reseat the drive, and check in the board's manual whether this slot shares its lanes with another device.

data.name: Check_DriveSlotLimited
data.value: The M.2 slot limits the SSD

data.name: Check_DriveSlotLimited_Text
data.value: The slot is narrower, or of an older PCIe generation, than the drive, so the drive's top sequential speed is cut. That is how this slot is built; another M.2 slot on the board may be faster.

data.name: Check_DriveLinkBelowDrive
data.value: The SSD runs at fewer lanes than it supports

data.name: Check_DriveLinkBelowDrive_Text
data.value: The drive runs at fewer lanes than it supports; how many the slot provides could not be read. Some M.2 slots (often the chipset's) give only x2: see the board's manual.

data.name: Check_BenchBelowPeers
data.value: Slower than usual for this model

data.name: Check_BenchBelowPeers_Text
data.value: This result is below the usual result of other systems with the same part. The numbers beside it, and the line under it, show what differs.

data.name: Check_BenchWithPeers_Text
data.value: This result is within the usual range of other systems with the same part.

data.name: Check_BenchFewPeers
data.value: Too few systems to compare with

data.name: Check_BenchFewPeers_Text
data.value: Fewer than three systems with this part have been measured, so what is normal for it is not known yet. The result is kept and counts towards the comparison lists.

data.name: Check_Hint_OnBattery
data.value: The machine was on battery during the run: plug the charger in and run it again.

data.name: Check_Hint_PowerSteady
data.value: Power held steady under load, so the all-core clock is set by the power limit (the BIOS's, or the laptop maker's): a setting, not a fault.

data.name: Check_Hint_LessPowerThanPeers
data.value: This part drew clearly less power than the typical system without getting hotter: a lower power limit is set (a BIOS profile such as Intel's default settings, or the laptop's). Not a fault; raise the limit in the BIOS if more speed is wanted and the cooling allows it.

data.name: Check_Hint_HotterThanPeers
data.value: This part ran clearly hotter than the typical system: its cooling is the likely cause.

data.name: Check_Hint_LowerClockThanPeers
data.value: Its clock was clearly lower than the typical system's at similar power and heat: check the power plan, the BIOS settings and the other findings here.

data.name: Web_Peers_Last
data.value: slower than all {0} models in the list

data.name: Web_Peers_First
data.value: faster than all {0} models in the list

data.name: Check_CpuBelowBoost
data.value: The CPU does not reach its boost clock

data.name: Check_CpuBelowBoost_Text
data.value: With one busy thread the fastest core stayed well under the single-core boost its maker publishes for this model. Check the power plan (maximum processor state, boost mode), the BIOS (boost settings, a fixed multiplier) and, on a laptop, the charger and the power mode.

data.name: Check_CpuPowerLimit_Text
data.value: The power the processor settled at under all-core load, next to the figures Intel publishes for this model. The line under it names the setting in use.

data.name: Check_Hint_PowerAtBaseSpec
data.value: The long-term limit equals Intel's Processor Base Power for this model: a default or Baseline-type setting in the BIOS. The processor is fine; its all-core clock is lower by that setting's design.

data.name: Check_Hint_PowerAtTurboSpec
data.value: The limit equals Intel's Maximum Turbo Power for this model: Intel's default performance setting.

data.name: Check_Hint_PowerAboveSpec
data.value: The processor drew more than Intel's Maximum Turbo Power for this model: the board's BIOS lifts Intel's limits. That gives more clock and much more heat; for Core 13th and 14th gen desktop processors Intel recommends its default power settings and the latest BIOS (microcode).
